evidence_quotes.quote: Empirical material is drawn from fieldwork carried out in March 2013 and March 2015. A focus group discussion with project beneficiaries consisting of women’s savings group members was held in Chamazi in March 2013. This was followed by in-depth interviews with 17 evicted households who resettled in Chamazi.

Notwithstanding this, the community registered its newly acquired land under one block title with the Ministry of Lands, Housing and Human Settlements. The block title as a form of collective landholding model meant that every community member had an equal stake in the ownership of the newly purchased land in Chamazi.

The insecure land occupancy status in Kurasini deprived residents of their citizenship rights and access to basic infrastructure. In essence, they were alienated and marginalized by both the state and market forces in the provision of water and sanitation, leaving them to their own devices.

Initially, the borehole water was used for house construction purposes free of charge, before the community instituted a small fee for onward domestic use. The water is pumped into an overhead tank before it is distributed to individual households through pipe networks.

However, in the Chamazi case, the block title dissolved the marginal socioeconomic difference between tenants and landlords, giving equitable use rights to all members. Recognizing the intricacies of the tenure arrangement and its linkage with service provision, the community settled for a block title that would put all members on an equal social standing.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community drinking-water and sanitation/sewerage service access among low-income residents evicted from the Kurasini informal settlement and resettled in the peri-urban Chamazi settlement in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Plain reading: clearly examines urban governance, participatory citizenship, legally registered community federation rules, and state-community institutional relations in water and sanitation provision. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: while part of the case involves grassroots savings and NGO-supported off-grid project delivery, Sections III, IV.a, and IV.c explicitly analyze rule-type tenure, registration, and administrative accommodation mechanisms directly governing infrastructure investment and household service access — specifically (1) how informal occupancy insecurity and tenant-versus-landlord legal rules in Kurasini excluded residents from public/market water and sanitation provision and state compensation, (2) institutional accommodation by the Ministry of Lands, Housing and Human Settlements of an unprecedented collective block-title land registration in Chamazi that equalized former tenants' rights and unlocked NGO/municipal water and sanitation investment, (3) residential land certification and site layout approval by Temeke Municipal Council, and (4) legal registration of the federation's constitution and community fee rules for household water and sewer connections.
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative empirical case study based on primary fieldwork conducted in March 2013 and March 2015, including a focus group discussion with women's savings group beneficiaries, in-depth interviews with 17 resettled evicted households, semi-structured interviews with 4 DAWASA and Temeke Municipal Council officials, structured interviews with 2 CCI NGO officials, field observation, and project document review.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports concrete qualitative and descriptive service-access outcomes: transition from vendor dependence, shallow wells, illegal pipe connections, and open sewage drains in Kurasini to piped domestic water distribution from a solar-powered borehole and overhead tank, central water point sales to unconnected neighbouring households, and underground household sewer pipe connections to an on-site wastewater treatment plant in Chamazi, alongside equitable access for former tenants.
criterion_notes.c5: Population (approximately 300 evicted tenant households resettled from Kurasini to Chamazi in Dar es Salaam; fieldwork sample of 17 households, 1 focus group, and 6 institutional/NGO officials; household and community/settlement units of analysis), exposure (tenure security, collective block-title registration, municipal residential certification/planning approval, legally registered community federation governance, and community fee rules), outcome (household piped water and decentralized sewer connections and equitable access), and qualitative case-study design are clearly identifiable.

study_design: Qualitative case study (multidisciplinary interpretive approach using focus group discussion, in-depth household interviews, semi-structured and structured official/NGO interviews, field observation, and document review)
population_and_sample: Low-income evicted tenant households (~300 households in a slum-dweller federation) relocated from Kurasini informal settlement to Chamazi peri-urban settlement in Temeke Municipality, Dar es Salaam, Tanzania (primary fieldwork sample: 1 focus group discussion with women's savings group members, 17 evicted households resettled in Chamazi, 4 DAWASA and Temeke Municipal Council officials, and 2 Centre for Community Initiatives officials; settlement and household units of analysis).
exposure: Land tenure and administrative registration/certification rules and community governance institutions: informal occupancy insecurity and tenant legal status in Kurasini versus formal collective block-title registration with the Ministry of Lands, Housing and Human Settlements, residential land certification and site layout approval by Temeke Municipal Council, legal registration of the community federation's constitution, and community fee rules for water and sewer connections in Chamazi.
outcome: Household and community water and sanitation access: piped household domestic water supply from a solar-powered borehole and overhead tank, standpipe water sales to neighbouring unconnected households, underground household sewer connections to a decentralized wastewater treatment plant, and elimination of landlord-tenant exclusion from services.
rationale: Wamuchiru (2017) is an empirical qualitative case study in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, drawing on fieldwork from 2013 and 2015 (focus group discussion, 17 household interviews, 6 municipal/utility/NGO interviews, observation, and document review). Although the Chamazi water and sewerage systems were built off-grid through grassroots mobilization and NGO partnerships beyond DAWASA's network, the paper explicitly analyzes rule-type legal and administrative mechanisms governing service provision and access (especially in Section IV.c): how insecure tenure and tenant legal status prevented formal service access in Kurasini, and how negotiating an unprecedented collective block-title land registration with the Ministry of Lands, obtaining formal residential certification and layout approval from Temeke Municipal Council, legally registering a federation constitution, and setting community user/connection fees enabled piped water and decentralized sewer connections and eliminated landlord-tenant exclusion. Qualitative socio-legal/institutional studies of tenure and accommodation mechanisms are eligible for the systematic review's mechanism synthesis under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings of Criterion 2. Confidence is medium because the physical water and sanitation infrastructure was community/NGO co-produced rather than a direct public utility network extension, though tenure registration and municipal certification were directly analyzed as preconditions enabling access.
